The game was great but i stopped playing it since every update the game got more buggy and unbalanced. All the stuff you could archive without paying real money was made much more difficult, unless you plan to take years non stop grinding or paying huge ammounts of money you will realisticly never finish the techtree. At some point the ingame events needed you to play around 2 hours a day for a week and you where able to miss a few days for unlocking the vehicles, now you better have nothing else to do as paying for the whole time, even unlocking missed milestones got 5 times more expensive. Premium vehicles went form around 60€ to >100€. Almost all new premium vehicles have an advantage, just to somehow get neved shortly before the next overpowerded premium gets put into the game. 

TLDR:
-premium vehicles are expensive and give you and edge over normal palyers
-playing without buying premium accounts is just waisting your time yince you get way less xp
-grind ist way to much for higher br ground vehicles, aircrafts are faster to grind, but in higer tiers your default loadouts so bad you have little chance against a player that unlocked all the weapons already.
-event vehicles have crazy requirements, dont have a job for some of those grind events or you have to pay money
-if you play the game for fun and dont expect to go fast into the high tiers its still good and fun to play, but the negatives outweight the positives in my oppinion (moslty if your game gets ruined by someone who payed to have an advantage, some brs are so bad no skill you have can make you win those encounters).

[h1]I would not recommend this game to new players.[/h1]
Having a predatory monetisation and a monopoly in the space it resides (sim-cade, not quite boring mil-sim, not quite ardadey shooter equivalent of tank world), makes it something you should avoid playing if you are not into the military vehicles (like you might be able to tell I am into, given the amount of hours). The grind is immense, yes, but it would not be too bad if it wasn't for the plethora of issues alongside. 

[h3]There is a definitive bias towards certain vehicles.[/h3] Usually it is just tech trees which the majority of people play (so bring more casual players which brings the stats down and as Gaijin balances purely off of stat sheets, that becomes a problem) and screws over small nations. This can also happen with premiums (because money obviously) and much needed changes (like BMPT) are done extremely slowly, (or in the case of the T58) barely at all. There is also a point where Gaijin selectively looks at historical documents (obviously not talking about secret documents, they aren't followed for obvious reasons) for the sake of balancing reasons. Take the Abrams. Yes it can be a bit murky when it comes to its hull armour but the general consensus is that it does not need an armour buff to make it impenetrable like all the US mains want it to be. There are tanks such as the chinese MBTs (ZTZ-99 I think?) with a 60mm lower front plate or the british challenger tanks with a 70mm lower front plate (they also have a fictional turret basket which does not exist for some reason?), yet those aren't nearly talked about as much. Also this is from personal experience, but please just remove the fictional APHE belt from the yak-9K and move it back down in BR. Also raise the BR of the Me-262 with the 50mm APHE.

[h3]Some decisions are also agnostic of nations and just feel oppressive.[/h3] Close air support, for example in ground realistic battles. Unless someone sacrifices their spawn of a tank in a [b][u]tank[/u][/b] gamemode to become an SPAA permenantly defending, there is not much one can do. And when there are multiple planes? There isn't anything to do either. At higher tiers, from what I have heard it is usually the case where the AA systems get massively more powerful but so do the aircraft, widening the gap between "we have 1 guy who is just sitting in an SPAA doing nothing for the team and getting maybe 1 kill" and "our whole team just got wiped by one guy". This problem is made worse by anti radiation missiles recently added.

[h3]The game engine itself is also quite buggy[/h3](I don't know if this is just a me problem but sometimes it will black screen and I can tell the game is still running because the audio is still running, yet I have to restart my PC in the middle of the match. Occassionally there are stutters which are annoying and make me think it could black screen but it is only for a moment. When the engine works, it works very well and I can get hundreds of frames on a budget card while looking good. Sometimes the sound bugs out though I guess too.

I have been putting off this review for a little while, also by the EULA changes making it easier to ban people for leaving negative reviews (do with that information what you want). After the immensley steep learning curve, I found quite a bit of the game fun, its just lots of the other aspects either need work, or the game will just die. A little bit more transparency with the community might be appreciated as well.

Seven hundred and forty-six days.

That is not just a number. 746 days of continuous access to War Thunder isn't a milestone; it’s a self-inflicted prison sentence. It’s a pact with the devil signed in blood, sweat, and Silver Lions. It means that for over two years of your biological existence, there has not been a single day where your mind was not claimed by the Grind.

War Thunder is a masterpiece of cognitive dissonance. It is a beautifully unnerving digital black hole that slowly extracts your soul while whispering in your ear that the next match will be the one where you finally dominate.

The horror of this game lies in its brutal, mathematical precision. You sit there, commanding a tank modeled down to the millimeter of historical accuracy. The tension is palpable. The engine rumbles beneath your hull. You advance with hyper-vigilant caution, checking every corner, every bush, every pixelated treeline. There is a poetic, breathtaking beauty in the way the morning sun cuts through the fog on a rolling European hill. You feel powerful. You feel like a commander.

And then, out of nowhere. One millisecond.

No warning. Just the deafening crack of an APFSDS shell that traveled three kilometers across the map, punched through your frontal armor, detonated your ammo rack, and turned your highly trained crew into a cloud of vaporized pixels. The kill-cam forces you to watch the flawless physics of your own destruction. It is pure psychological violence. The game calmly looks you in the eyes and says, "You miscalculated by two centimeters. Back to the hangar."

And that is exactly where the addiction takes its hold. It is a sickness.

Because after you alt-F4 out of the game, swearing on your ancestors that you are deleting it for good, twenty-four hours pass. The daily reward timer resets. That green desktop icon stares back at you. You think about your 746-day streak. If you don’t log in today, the counter dies. It goes back to zero. And you cannot let it die. That number has become a part of your identity.

So you boot it up again. You listen to the hauntingly familiar hangar music. You strap yourself back into the cockpit of a jet fighter. Your radar is screaming, your RWR warning tones are piercing your eardrums, and surface-to-air missiles are carving white scars into the sky all around you. There is a raw, primal adrenaline in surviving that absolute hell. When you pull off that perfect leading shot, when your shell penetrates the one weak spot of an enemy heavy tank, your brain releases a hit of dopamine so violent that you instantly forget the previous fifteen minutes of agonizing suffering.

War Thunder despises you, and you worship it for it. It destroys your nervous system, drains your free time, and forces you to study Cold War military manuals like you're preparing for a university exam. Yet, here you are. 746 days later, hand gripped tight on the mouse, staring into the abyss of the screen.

The biggest problem with War Thunder is its matchmaking. There is basically no skill-based matchmaking, so completely new players can be thrown into games against players with thousands or even tens of thousands of battles.

Battle Rating alone does not make a fair match when one player knows every map, vehicle weakness and strategy while the other is still learning the game.

Getting destroyed by highly experienced players over and over again is extremely frustrating and can make new players quit before they even have a chance to enjoy the game. War Thunder desperately needs a better matchmaking system based on player experience or skill, not just vehicle BR.
